prompt: A straight line on log-log axes means what kind of law?

options.html: A straight line: loss falls by the same amount for each unit of compute.
An exponential: loss falls by the same factor for each unit of compute.
A power law: loss falls by the same factor each time compute is multiplied by the same factor.
No law at all; log axes distort everything.

explain: A power law, L=C x−pL = C\,x^{-p}L=Cx−p. Taking logarithms, log⁡L=log⁡C−plog⁡x\log L = \log C - p \log xlogL=logC−plogx: a straight line in log⁡x\log xlogx with slope −p-p−p. Scaling laws for language models (L11, M35) are exactly such lines.

prompt: Why does a logarithm turn multiplication into addition, and why is that useful for probabilities?
answer: A logarithm is an exponent: log_b x is the power of b that gives x. Multiplying numbers adds their exponents, b^u b^v = b^(u+v), so the log of a product is the sum of the logs. Probabilities of independent events multiply and quickly become too small to store; their logs add instead, staying modest in size and turning products of thousands of terms into sums.
